source.title: Characterizing Datapoints via Second-Split Forgetting
source.authors: Pratyush Maini; S. Garg; Zachary Chase Lipton; J. Kolter

record.tranche_reason: The study compares learning and forgetting of clean and mislabeled examples, finding that their first-split learning times can overlap and that this depends on the optimizer.
record.gate_note: The paper reports experiments with 10% randomly flipped labels and first-split training to 100% training accuracy. It does not test fitting a completely random labeling, noise fractions from none to all, or shuffled/noise inputs. AUC results for label-noise detection and generalization after removing examples are not rows for these claim versions.
record.test_reason: The study directly compares clean and randomly mislabeled examples' learning times. Its results qualify V6: learning order overlaps substantially and depends on the optimizer and the complexity of clean examples.
record.authors_conclusion: The record's paraphrase is accurate. The authors present first-split learning and second-split forgetting as complementary: late learning can characterize useful rare or complex examples as well as mislabeled examples, while rapid second-split forgetting helps identify mislabeled examples. Their learning-time separation is optimizer dependent.
record.recipe_differences: The study uses two data splits and tracks example learning and forgetting times; it does not reproduce the original random-label fitting experiment.
record.method_sensitivity: The distinction in first-split learning times depends on optimizer: SGD provides some separation, while Adam jointly learns many clean and mislabeled samples.

fits_no_version.finding: During second-split training, mislabeled examples are generally forgotten faster than clean, rare, or complex examples; this separation depends on learning rate and subgroup frequency.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Forgetting after training on a held-out partition can distinguish types of example hardness.

record.problems: The relevant evidence uses 10% label noise rather than fully random labels. First-split learning-time results are primarily qualitative descriptions of plotted distributions; uncertainty for these comparisons is not stated.
record.rows_left_out: No other qualifying results for the tested version were reported. The AUC noise-detection results and example-removal generalization results measure other outcomes and are not rows for V6.

untested.parts: Fitting completely random labels, chance test performance, and keeping architecture and training hyperparameters unchanged relative to true-label training.
The training-time ratio between true and random labels and convergence across corruption fractions.
Fitting shuffled pixels, independently permuted pixels, or unstructured Gaussian-noise inputs.
Perfect training fit and steadily worsening test error across a corruption sweep from none to all.
Controlled comparisons of regularization or augmentation for random-label fitting and true-label generalization.
Direct measurement of shared-feature acquisition versus example-specific memorization; comparisons with a completely randomly labeled dataset.

record.verdict_notes: This study is not an original source. The 100% training-accuracy procedure with 10% label corruption does not establish V1 or V4. Noise-detection AUC and cleansing performance are excluded as detection and downstream outcomes. R1 and R4 describe complementary aspects of the SGD result, rather than independent replications.

versions.untested_parts: Completely random labeling of the training set and test error at chance.
Training-time cost relative to true labels and convergence as corruption fraction changes.
Shuffled pixels, independently permuted pixels, and Gaussian-noise inputs.
A sweep from no corruption to all labels corrupted, with training and test error measured.
Whether regularization or augmentation prevents fitting random labels or affects true-label generalization.

The study does not measure a complete sequence of learning shared patterns followed by memorization; its evidence concerns first-split learning times and second-split forgetting for partially corrupted data.

rows.subject: ResNet-9
rows.operation_detail: Compared first-split learning times of clean and mislabeled examples.

conditions.value: 10% randomly changed to an incorrect class

rows.value: A large fraction of mislabeled and correctly labeled examples are learned at the same time.
rows.note: Textual result; the paper also says a large fraction of clean examples are never forgotten during second-split training.
rows.check: The result is accurate. Learning time means the earliest epoch after which an example remains correctly classified, rather than its first correct prediction.

source_check.locator_found: Section 4.3, Figure 3a and accompanying paragraph; Section 4.1 specifies ResNet-9 and SGD.

rows.subject: ResNet-9
rows.operation_detail: Compared first-split learning times of clean and mislabeled examples in the combined dataset.
rows.value: A high fraction of CIFAR-10 (complex) samples learn at the same speed as mislabeled samples.
rows.note: The paper describes CIFAR-10 as the complex examples in this setting.
rows.check: Specify the four-class union: MNIST digits 0–3 and four CIFAR-10 classes mapped to the same labels, with 10% label noise in each dataset. The overlap concerns complex clean CIFAR-10 examples.

source_check.locator_found: Section 4.3, Figure 3b and accompanying paragraph; Appendix C, Complex Examples, specifies the four-class union.

rows.subject: ResNet-9
rows.operation_detail: Compared clean and mislabeled examples' learning times under a changed optimizer.
rows.value: Adam results in joint learning of a large fraction of both mislabeled and clean samples.
rows.note: The authors report very low separation between clean and mislabeled samples with Adam.
rows.check: The authors report very low separation, rather than quantitatively establishing zero separation. Substantial joint learning limits the proposed temporal ordering.

source_check.locator_found: Appendix C.1, Stability across optimizers, Figure 7; Sections 4.1 and B.1 specify default architecture and noise procedure.

rows.subject: ResNet-9
rows.operation_detail: Compared clean and mislabeled examples' learning times under SGD.
rows.value: Mislabeled samples are learnt slower than a large fraction of the training examples.
rows.note: The paper says this gives the learning-time metric some degree of separation between clean and mislabeled examples.
rows.check: The stated comparison directly shows delayed learning of mislabeled examples relative to a large fraction of training examples. This supports the ordering for that comparison; R1 records its incomplete coverage.

source_check.locator_found: Appendix C.1, Stability across optimizers, Figure 7.
